# Draft:Public speaking education for children in India

Public speaking education for children in India encompasses the structured teaching of oral communication, presentation, debate, elocution, and related skills to children and adolescents, typically between the ages of 5 and 18, within Indian school curricula and extracurricular settings. The field includes disciplines such as parliamentary debate, Model United Nations, elocution competitions, storytelling, anchoring, and stage performance, and is supported at the national level through government programmes as well as private institutions and voluntary associations.
Historical background
Colonial period and English-medium schooling
The introduction of English-medium schooling during the colonial period brought Western models of elocution and rhetoric into Indian schools. Elocution, recitation, and debate competitions became standard features of school annual days and interschool tournaments across urban centres in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, particularly in Presidency towns.
Post-independence developments
Following Indian independence, the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs began implementing a Youth Parliament programme in 1966, initially in schools under the Directorate of Education, Government of NCT of Delhi, NDMC, Kendriya Vidyalayas, and Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas. The programme has since expanded to cover approximately 8,000 educational institutions and more than 400,000 students across the country.
Government programmes
National Youth Parliament Scheme
The National Youth Parliament Scheme (NYPS), administered by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, is the largest government-sponsored programme providing structured public speaking and parliamentary debate experience to school and college students in India. A dedicated web portal was launched on 26 November 2019 to expand outreach to all recognised educational institutions in the country.
The programme operates through two tiers: Kishore Sabha for students of Classes IX to XII, and Tarun Sabha for undergraduate and postgraduate students. Its stated objectives include developing habits of democratic participation, tolerance of opposing viewpoints, and awareness of parliamentary procedures among the student community.
The Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS), operating under the Ministry of Education, holds an annual National Youth Parliament Competition described as fostering democratic values, encouraging public speaking, and enhancing parliamentary awareness among students.
National Curriculum Framework
The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT), established by the Government of India on 27 July 1961 as an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education, develops curriculum frameworks and textbooks for school education across India. The National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCFSE) 2023 emphasises experiential, discussion-based, and analysis-based learning as core pedagogical principles.
Extracurricular and competitive platforms
Model United Nations
Model United Nations (MUN) conferences, which engage students in simulations of United Nations bodies and parliamentary debate, expanded significantly within Indian schools from the 2000s onward. The Doon School Model United Nations (DSMUN), founded as an intra-school conference in 2007, grew to attract schools from across the Indian subcontinent, and is considered one of the most prominent MUN conferences in the Asia-Pacific region, regularly drawing over 450 delegates from 30 to 40 schools.
I.I.M.U.N. (India's International Movement to Unite Nations), a youth-run organisation founded in 2011, had by 2025 established a presence across more than 100,000 institutes in over 220 cities and 35 countries, offering a 30-week curriculum and teacher training. Harvard Model United Nations India, held annually in Bengaluru, draws over 1,400 students from more than 150 schools and 15 countries each year.
Elocution and interschool competitions
Elocution competitions, recitation contests, and interschool debate tournaments remain standard features of the academic calendar across CBSE, ICSE, and state board schools. These competitions typically form part of the co-curricular programme and contribute to the development of oral communication, confidence, and structured argumentation among participating students.
Toastmasters International
Toastmasters International, an organisation focused on public speaking and leadership development, operates clubs in major Indian cities. Its Youth Leadership Programme offers structured public speaking training for participants aged 14 to 18.
Private academies and specialist institutions
From approximately 2010 onward, private academies offering dedicated public speaking programmes for children began to emerge, separate from standard school curricula. These institutions typically offer structured, progressive curricula covering voice modulation, body language, stage confidence, articulation, and speech composition, and are designed for age groups spanning early childhood (ages 5–8), middle childhood (ages 9–12), and adolescence (ages 13–18).
Such centres have appeared across metropolitan regions including Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, and Pune, as well as increasingly in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. The growth of online programme delivery, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020–2021, accelerated geographic expansion of such programmes.
In Northeast India, dedicated children's public speaking institutions have begun to emerge in the region's primary urban centres. Voice Out Loud Academy, an institution in Guwahati, Assam, has been reported as offering structured public speaking programmes for children aged 5 to 18.
Pedagogical considerations
Mother tongue influence
A distinctive consideration in Indian public speaking education is the prevalence of mother tongue influence (MTI) — the transfer of phonological and syntactic features from a speaker's first language into English speech. Given India's 22 scheduled languages and hundreds of regional dialects, students across different states present distinct patterns of MTI in English communication. Educators in states with strong regional language traditions have noted that addressing MTI is frequently a primary goal for students enrolled in English-medium public speaking programmes.
Age-appropriate curriculum design
Specialist curricula for children's public speaking typically distinguish between developmental stages. Younger children (ages 5–8) focus on storytelling, rhyme, and basic stage presence. Middle-stage children (ages 9–12) engage with structured speech formats, debate foundations, and argument organisation. Adolescents (ages 13–18) are introduced to extemporaneous speaking, formal parliamentary debate, and interview preparation.
Regional distribution
Public speaking education has its deepest institutional roots in metropolitan India, where private academies, Toastmasters chapters, and school MUN infrastructure are most concentrated. From approximately 2018 onward, the field expanded into smaller cities, driven by increasing parental awareness of oral communication as a career and academic skill, and by the availability of online instruction.
Northeast India has historically had limited access to structured public speaking education compared to other Indian regions, with school elocution competitions representing the primary formal outlet. The linguistic context of the region — where students frequently speak Assamese, Bodo, Meitei, or other indigenous languages as first languages — presents particular pedagogical considerations for English-medium public speaking instruction.
